claim: RhopH2 is one of ~15 known proteins that localize to the rhoptry bulb in Plasmodium merozoites.
source: RhopH2 is one of ~15 known proteins that localize to the rhoptry bulb in Plasmodium merozoites (Counihan et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Counihan et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2003)

claim: RhopH2 is found in a high molecular weight complex with RhopH1 and RhopH3.
source: It is found in a high molecular weight complex with RhopH1 and RhopH3 (Cooper et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper et al., 1988

claim: The RhopH complex is discharged from merozoites and associates with the erythrocyte surface upon merozoite contact.
source: that is discharged from merozoites, associating with the erythrocyte surface upon merozoite contact (Sam-Yellowe et al., 1988; Sam-Yellowe and Perkins, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Sam-Yellowe et al., 1988; Sam-Yellowe and Perkins, 1991)

claim: Multiple localizations including the PV membrane, Maurer's clefts and the cytosolic face of the erythrocyte membrane have been described for RhopH protein constituents.
source: The localization of RhopH proteins in the newly-infected erythrocyte is less clear as multiple localizations, including the PV membrane (PVM), Maurer's clefts and the cytosolic face of the erythrocyte membrane have been described for its constituents using different experimental approaches (Perkins and Ziefer, 1994; Ndengele et al., 1995; Sam-Yellowe et al., 2001; Hiller et al., 2003; Vincensini et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies using different experimental approaches

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are each encoded by a single gene.
source: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are each encoded by a single gene.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: RhopH1 in P. falciparum is encoded by a multi-gene family comprising five variant genes termed clag 2, 3.1, 3.2, 8 and 9.
source: In contrast, RhopH1 in P. falciparum, the most pathogenic of the species infecting humans, is encoded by a multi-gene family comprising five variant genes termed clag 2, 3.1, 3.2, 8 and 9 (with clag3.1 and 3.2 mutually exclusively transcribed) (Gupta et al., 2015; Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005; Ling et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Gupta et al., 2015; Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005; Ling et al., 2004)

claim: Clag3.1 and 3.2 are mutually exclusively transcribed.
source: In contrast, RhopH1 in P. falciparum, the most pathogenic of the species infecting humans, is encoded by a multi-gene family comprising five variant genes termed clag 2, 3.1, 3.2, 8 and 9 (with clag3.1 and 3.2 mutually exclusively transcribed) (Gupta et al., 2015; Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005; Ling et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Clag3 has been linked to plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC) activity via a high throughput drug-screening approach.
source: Via a high throughput drug-screening approach Clag3 has been linked to plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC) activity (Nguitragool et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguitragool et al., 2011

claim: PSAC is a type of new permeability pathway (NPP) induced in the erythrocyte membrane by Plasmodium spp. that increases the cell's porosity to organic and inorganic solutes.
source: PSAC is a type of new permeability pathway (NPP) induced in the erythrocyte membrane by Plasmodium spp. that increases the cell's porosity to organic and inorganic solutes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: P. falciparum Clag3 null-mutants exhibit delayed in vitro growth.
source: P. falciparum Clag3 null-mutants exhibit delayed in vitro growth, although NPP activity has not been investigated (Comeaux et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Comeaux et al., 2011

claim: Clag3 exhibits no homology to known ion channel proteins.
source: Intriguingly, Clag3 exhibits no homology to known ion channel proteins and lacks conventional membrane spanning regions to form a pore through the erythrocyte membrane, although it exists as both an integral and peripheral membrane protein in the infected erythrocyte (Nguitragool et al., 2011; Zainabadi, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nguitragool et al., 2011 and Zainabadi, 2016

claim: Clag3 lacks conventional membrane spanning regions to form a pore through the erythrocyte membrane.
source: Intriguingly, Clag3 exhibits no homology to known ion channel proteins and lacks conventional membrane spanning regions to form a pore through the erythrocyte membrane, although it exists as both an integral and peripheral membrane protein in the infected erythrocyte (Nguitragool et al., 2011; Zainabadi, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nguitragool et al., 2011 and Zainabadi, 2016

claim: Clag3 exists as both an integral and peripheral membrane protein in the infected erythrocyte.
source: Intriguingly, Clag3 exhibits no homology to known ion channel proteins and lacks conventional membrane spanning regions to form a pore through the erythrocyte membrane, although it exists as both an integral and peripheral membrane protein in the infected erythrocyte (Nguitragool et al., 2011; Zainabadi, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nguitragool et al., 2011 and Zainabadi, 2016

claim: Both the rhopH2 gene and rhopH3 gene are refractory to deletion.
source: Both the rhopH2 gene and rhopH3 gene are refractory to deletion (Cowman et al., 2000; Janse et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowman et al., 2000 and Janse et al., 2011

claim: Diagnostic PCR of transfectants resistant to WR99210 selection confirmed that transgenic parasites harbored the expected integration event.
source: Diagnostic PCR of transfectants resistant to WR99210 selection after three rounds of drug cycling confirmed that transgenic parasites, termed PfRhopH2-HAglmS, harbored the expected integration event (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: RhopH2 typically runs at 140 kDa by SDS-PAGE.
source: RhopH2 typically runs at 140 kDa by SDS-PAGE (Cooper et al., 1988; Ling et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cooper et al., 1988 and Ling et al., 2003

claim: The observed 150 kDa band of RhopH2-HA is consistent with its anticipated size.
source: and the observed 150 kDa band of RhopH2-HA is consistent with its anticipated size (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and inference from the addition of epitope tags

claim: RhopH2-HA localized to the rhoptry and co-localized with other rhoptry bulb proteins, RhopH1, RhopH3 and RAMA.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis (IFA) confirmed RhopH2-HA localized to the rhoptry and co-localized with other rhoptry bulb proteins, RhopH1, RhopH3 and RAMA but not with the rhoptry neck protein, RON4, the micronemal marker, AMA-1 or the plasma membrane protein MSP1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1d

claim: RhopH2-HA did not co-localize with the rhoptry neck protein RON4, the micronemal marker AMA-1, or the plasma membrane protein MSP1.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis (IFA) confirmed RhopH2-HA localized to the rhoptry and co-localized with other rhoptry bulb proteins, RhopH1, RhopH3 and RAMA but not with the rhoptry neck protein, RON4, the micronemal marker, AMA-1 or the plasma membrane protein MSP1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1d

claim: The addition of the epitope tags and ribozyme sequence did not impact on RhopH2-HAglmS to grow normally.
source: Comparison of the wildtype 3D7 and RhopH2-HAglmS parasite lines revealed that the addition of the epitope tags and ribozyme sequence did not impact on RhopH2-HAglmS to grow normally (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by growth comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Western blot analysis revealed weak expression of RhopH2 during the ring and trophozoite stages, with a peak of expression at schizont stage.
source: Western blot analysis revealed weak expression of RhopH2 during the ring and trophozoite stages, with a peak of expression at schizont stage (Figure 2a)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2a

claim: RhopH2 expression pattern is in keeping with when RhopH2 is maximally transcribed.
source: in keeping with when RhopH2 is maximally transcribed (Ling et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ling et al., 2003

claim: RhopH2 synthesized during schizogony is carried in during invasion and localizes to the interface between the parasite and host cell.
source: IFA confirmed RhopH2 synthesized during schizogony is carried in during invasion and localizes to the interface between the parasite and host cell (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Weak labeling of RhopH2 could be observed at the erythrocyte membrane.
source: Weak labeling could also be observed at the erythrocyte membrane.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations described in the text

claim: As the parasite matured, RhopH2 could be detected in the erythrocyte cytoplasm, often exhibiting distinct punctate labeling.
source: As the parasite matured, RhopH2 could be detected in the erythrocyte cytoplasm, often exhibiting distinct punctate labeling, and the intensity of labeling at the erythrocyte membrane became more pronounced.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations described in the text

claim: The intensity of RhopH2 labeling at the erythrocyte membrane became more pronounced as the parasite matured.
source: As the parasite matured, RhopH2 could be detected in the erythrocyte cytoplasm, often exhibiting distinct punctate labeling, and the intensity of labeling at the erythrocyte membrane became more pronounced.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations described in the text

claim: RhopH2 did not co-localize with SBP1, a Maurer's cleft resident protein.
source: RhopH2 did not co-localize with SBP1, a Maurer's cleft resident protein, indicating RhopH2 is not trafficked to the erythrocyte membrane via these membranous structures as previously suggested (Sam-Yellowe et al., 2001; Vincensini et al., 2005) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2c

claim: RhopH2 is not trafficked to the erythrocyte membrane via Maurer's clefts.
source: RhopH2 did not co-localize with SBP1, a Maurer's cleft resident protein, indicating RhopH2 is not trafficked to the erythrocyte membrane via these membranous structures as previously suggested (Sam-Yellowe et al., 2001; Vincensini et al., 2005) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of co-localization with SBP1 shown in Figure 2c

claim: The majority of RhopH2 could be extracted with carbonate when sequential solubility assays were conducted.
source: We found that in contrast to EXP2, which is a component of the Plasmodium translocon of exported proteins (PTEX) that resides at the PVM and requires Triton X-100 to be extracted from the membranes (de Koning-Ward et al., 2009), the majority of RhopH2 could already be extracted with carbonate when sequential solubility assays were conducted (Figure 2d, top panel).
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 2d

claim: RhopH2 is peripherally associated with membranes and is not an integral membrane protein.
source: This indicates that RhopH2 is peripherally associated with membranes and is not an integral membrane protein.
evidence: Inferred from the carbonate extraction data

claim: When resuspended directly in various detergents/buffers, RhopH2 could be extracted with carbonate and mostly with urea, whereas it remained in the Triton X-100 pellet fraction.
source: However, when erythrocytes infected with ring-stage parasites were saponin-lysed, pelleted by centrifugation and resuspended directly (rather than sequentially) in various detergents/buffers, RhopH2 could be extracted with carbonate and mostly with urea (which also extracts peripheral membrane proteins), whereas it remained in the Triton X-100 pellet fraction (Figure 2d, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by solubility assay data shown in Figure 2d

claim: RhopH2 predominantly has a peripheral association with the membranes at its respective locations.
source: Combined, this data indicates that while RhopH2 predominantly has a peripheral association with the membranes at its respective locations, RhopH2 may be interacting with erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins or is present in lipid rafts during the ring-stages, leading to its insolubility in Triton X-100 when resuspended in this buffer directly.
evidence: Inferred from the combined solubility assay data

claim: RhopH2 may be interacting with erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins or is present in lipid rafts during the ring-stages.
source: Combined, this data indicates that while RhopH2 predominantly has a peripheral association with the membranes at its respective locations, RhopH2 may be interacting with erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins or is present in lipid rafts during the ring-stages, leading to its insolubility in Triton X-100 when resuspended in this buffer directly.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the Triton X-100 insolubility data

claim: In both ring and trophozoite parasite stages, RhopH2 was pulled down as well as other members of the RhopH complex.
source: In both parasite stages, RhopH2 was pulled down as well as other members of the RhopH complex, relatively few PV proteins such the PTEX complex, many exported PEXEL proteins, especially in trophozoites, and a large number of erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, particularly in the ring stages (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Relatively few PV proteins such as the PTEX complex were pulled down with RhopH2.
source: In both parasite stages, RhopH2 was pulled down as well as other members of the RhopH complex, relatively few PV proteins such the PTEX complex, many exported PEXEL proteins, especially in trophozoites, and a large number of erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, particularly in the ring stages (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Many exported PEXEL proteins were pulled down with RhopH2, especially in trophozoites.
source: In both parasite stages, RhopH2 was pulled down as well as other members of the RhopH complex, relatively few PV proteins such the PTEX complex, many exported PEXEL proteins, especially in trophozoites, and a large number of erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, particularly in the ring stages (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: A large number of erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins were pulled down with RhopH2, particularly in the ring stages.
source: In both parasite stages, RhopH2 was pulled down as well as other members of the RhopH complex, relatively few PV proteins such the PTEX complex, many exported PEXEL proteins, especially in trophozoites, and a large number of erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, particularly in the ring stages (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: RhopH2 interacts with the other members of the RhopH complex, consistent with an earlier report demonstrating the RhopH complex persists intact for at least 18 hr post-invasion.
source: That RhopH2 was interacting with the other members of the RhopH complex (Figure 3c) is consistent with an earlier report demonstrating the RhopH complex persists intact for at least 18 hr post-invasion (Lustigman et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3c and citation to Lustigman et al., 1988

claim: There were more peptides recovered for RhopH1 and RhopH3 than there were for RhopH2 at the ring and trophozoite stages.
source: There were more peptides recovered for RhopH1 (particularly Clags3.1, 3.2 and 9) and RhopH3 than there were for RhopH2 at the ring and trophozoite stages (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Each component of the RhopH complex may not be in a 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Given that predicted molecular weights for the Clags (160–171 kDa) and RhopH2 (163 kDa) are similar but that of RhopH3 is somewhat smaller (104 kDa), this indicates that each component of the RhopH complex may not be in a 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: Inferred from the peptide recovery data and molecular weight considerations

claim: RhopH2 is present in a ~670 kDa complex that has a molecular mass larger than the predicted ~425 kDa.
source: Blue-Native PAGE gel analysis revealed that RhopH2 is present in a ~670 kDa complex that has a molecular mass larger than the predicted ~425 kDa (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 3d

claim: A smaller ~410 kDa complex containing RhopH2 was observed when using the zwitterionic detergent ASB-14.
source: We also observed a smaller ~410 kDa complex when using the zwitterionic detergent 3-(tetradecanoylamidopropyl dimethylammonio) propane 1-sulfonate (ASB-14), which could contain a subset of the RhopH proteins and/or other proteins (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 3d

claim: The most predominant peptides from known exported proteins included those of MESA, SEMP1, GBP130, PHIST proteins, and HSP70-x.
source: The most predominant peptides from known exported proteins included those of mature parasite-infected erythrocyte surface antigen (MESA; a protein that interacts with host protein 4.1) (Waller et al., 2003), small exported membrane protein 1 (SEMP1; a non-essential protein that localizes to the Maurer's clefts and is partially translocated to the erythrocyte membrane) (Dietz et al., 2014), glycophorin-binding protein 130 (GBP130; an exported soluble protein) (Maier et al., 2008), a variety of Plasmodium helical interspersed subtelomeric proteins (PHIST; some of which have been shown to interact with PfEMP1) (Proellocks et al., 2014; Oberli et al., 2014, 2016) and HSP70-x (localizes to J-dots) (Külzer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and citations to previous studies

claim: Peptides from exported proteins were more abundant in the pull-down performed on lysates from trophozoites compared to ring-stages.
source: Peptides from exported proteins were more abundant in the pull-down performed on lysates from trophozoites compared to ring-stages, in keeping with protein export peaking during the trophozoite stage.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and established knowledge about protein export timing

claim: More RESA peptides were observed in the ring-stage pull-down compared to trophozoite stage.
source: The exception was ring erythrocyte surface antigen (RESA) in which more peptides were observed in the ring-stage pull-down.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data

claim: RESA is one of the first proteins exported into the erythrocyte that ultimately localizes to the ankyrin-band 3 complex at the erythrocyte cytoskeleton.
source: RESA is one of the first proteins exported into the erythrocyte that ultimately localizes to the ankyrin-band 3 complex at the erythrocyte cytoskeleton.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: A large number of peptides to erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins were identified, including tubulin, spectrin, ankyrin, protein 4.1, band 3 and actin.
source: A large number of peptides to erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins were also identified, including tubulin, spectrin, ankyrin, protein 4.1, band 3 and actin (Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3f

claim: After invasion, the RhopH complex traffics from the PVM to the erythrocyte membrane.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that after invasion, the RhopH complex traffics from the PVM to the erythrocyte membrane and either en route or when it reaches its final destination, RhopH2 interacts with a number of exported parasite proteins that also bind to components of the host cytoskeleton.
evidence: Inferred from the combined immunoprecipitation and localization data

claim: RhopH2 interacts with a number of exported parasite proteins that also bind to components of the host cytoskeleton.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that after invasion, the RhopH complex traffics from the PVM to the erythrocyte membrane and either en route or when it reaches its final destination, RhopH2 interacts with a number of exported parasite proteins that also bind to components of the host cytoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data

claim: The addition of 2.5 mM GlcN resulted in knockdown of RhopH2 expression in schizonts by 84% within the first cycle.
source: RhopH2 is normally transcribed around the onset of schizogony (Ling et al., 2003; Bozdech et al., 2003; Le Roch et al., 2004) and the addition of 2.5 mM GlcN resulted in knockdown of RhopH2 expression in schizonts by 84% within the first cycle.
evidence: Supported by western blot data and densitometry analysis

claim: By late in the second cycle, RhopH2 protein levels were reduced by 92% in those parasites that made it to schizont stage.
source: By late in the second cycle, RhopH2 protein levels were reduced by 92% in those parasites that made it to schizont stage (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4a

claim: RhopH2-HAglmS parasites (+GlcN) appeared morphologically normal by the end of the first cycle.
source: RhopH2-HAglmS parasites (+GlcN) appeared morphologically normal by the end of the first cycle (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by Giemsa-stained smear data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The conversion of schizonts to ring stage parasites and invasion efficiency was not specifically affected by the knockdown of RhopH2.
source: In separate experiments whereby RhopH2-HAglmS parasites expressing GFP at the end of cycle one were incubated with donor erythrocytes, the conversion of schizonts to ring stage parasites and therefore invasion efficiency was not specifically affected by the knockdown of RhopH2 (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by FACS invasion assay data shown in Figure 4c

claim: A striking growth defect in RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) parasites was observed in the second cell cycle around the ring to trophozoite transition stage.
source: In contrast, a striking growth defect in RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) parasites was observed in the second cell cycle around the ring to trophozoite transition stage, with late-ring stage parasites appearing irregular in shape and trophozoites exhibiting an abnormal stunted phenotype rather than progressing to mature trophozoites (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by Giemsa-stained smear data shown in Figure 4b

claim: RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) parasites that transitioned to schizonts at the end of the second cycle harboured significantly lower numbers of merozoites per schizont.
source: In addition, RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) parasites that transitioned to schizonts at the end of the second cycle harboured significantly lower numbers of merozoites per schizont (mean of 19 merozoites cf 12 merozoites for –GlcN and +GlcN cultures, respectively p<0.0001) (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by merozoite counting data shown in Figure 4d with statistical analysis

claim: The time required to complete the second cycle and commence the third cycle was delayed in RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) parasites.
source: Moreover, the time required to complete the second cycle and commence the third cycle was delayed (~92 hr cf ~108 hr for -GlcN and +GlcN cultures, respectively) (Figure 4b,e).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4b and 4e

claim: There was ~4 fold reduction in the number of ring-stage parasites observed at the beginning of the third cycle when RhopH2 was knocked down.
source: This all translated to ~4 fold reduction in the number of ring-stage parasites observed at the beginning of the third cycle when compared to parasites not exposed to GlcN (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by parasitemia data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Growth of RhopH2-HAglmS parasites was significantly slower than 3D7 in all concentrations of GlcN by 36 hpi.
source: An unpaired t-test revealed RhopH2-HAglmS parasites grew significantly slower than 3D7 in all concentrations of GlcN by 36 hpi (p<0.01) (g)
evidence: Supported by pLDH assay data with statistical analysis

claim: Egress of RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) line was markedly delayed compared to 3D7 (+GlcN).
source: This revealed that egress of RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) line was markedly delayed compared to 3D7 (+GlcN) (p<0.001 for 2.5 mM GlcN) (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by nanoluciferase egress assay data shown in Figure 4g with statistical analysis

claim: The slower growth of RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) observed in cycle 2 is due to the specific effect of depletion of RhopH2 expression.
source: These results validate that the slower growth of RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) observed in cycle 2 is due to the specific effect of depletion of RhopH2 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results including controls

claim: No obvious differences were observed in general schizont morphology or in the ability of the erythrocyte to burst upon RhopH2 knockdown.
source: No obvious differences were observed in general schizont morphology or in the ability of the erythrocyte to burst, indicating egress per se was not actually affected.
evidence: Supported by video microscopy observations

claim: GlcN treatment caused the merozoites to remain clumped together after egress instead of dispersing rapidly.
source: Rather, instead of the merozoites dispersing rapidly after egress, GlcN treatment caused the merozoites to remain clumped together (Figure 5a, Videos 1–2), a phenotype not observed in 3D7 (+GlcN) parasites (not shown).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy data shown in Figure 5a and Videos 1-2

claim: Less than two merozoites per rupture were released and able to contact new erythrocytes after GlcN treatment compared with six merozoites without GlcN.
source: Nine and eleven schizont ruptures were observed ± GlcN treatment respectively, and as a consequence of merozoite clumping following GlcN treatment, less than two merozoites per rupture were released and able to contact new erythrocytes compared with six merozoites without GlcN (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Only 0.25 invasions per rupture occurred after GlcN treatment compared to 2.6 without treatment.
source: The net effect was fewer average invasions per rupture, with only 0.25 after GlcN treatment compared to 2.6 without treatment (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 5c

claim: 28 out of the 63 merozoites that made erythrocyte contact without GlcN went on to invade erythrocytes.
source: Whilst 28 out of the 63 merozoites that made erythrocyte contact without GlcN went on to invade erythrocytes (Figure 5d), only two out of the 14 merozoites treated with GlcN invaded erythrocytes, indicating a success rate of 0.44 and 0.14 invasions per contact, respectively (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 5d

claim: Only two out of the 14 merozoites treated with GlcN invaded erythrocytes.
source: Whilst 28 out of the 63 merozoites that made erythrocyte contact without GlcN went on to invade erythrocytes (Figure 5d), only two out of the 14 merozoites treated with GlcN invaded erythrocytes, indicating a success rate of 0.44 and 0.14 invasions per contact, respectively (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by video microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 5d

claim: The lower fold-increase in parasitemia from cycle two to the next after RhopH2 knockdown stemmed from a combined effect of reduction in the number of parasites reaching schizogony in cycle two and a reduced invasion rate.
source: From these results, it was inferred that the lower fold-increase in parasitemia from cycle two to the next after RhopH2 knockdown stemmed from a combined effect of reduction in the number of parasites reaching schizogony in cycle two and a reduced invasion rate.
evidence: Inferred from the combined video microscopy and growth data

claim: Transcription of rhoph2 in the PbRhopH2-iKD line was highly responsive to ATc, with ~11-fold reduction of rhoph2 mRNA in schizont stages.
source: Transcription of rhoph2 in this line, termed PbRhopH2-iKD, was highly responsive to ATc, with ~11-fold reduction of rhoph2 mRNA in schizont stages as determined by qRT-PCR and RT-PCR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d

claim: PbRhopH2-iKD parasites grew poorly in mice that had been pre-exposed to ATc 24 hr prior to infection.
source: PbRhopH2-iKD parasites grew poorly in mice that had been pre-exposed to ATc 24 hr prior to infection (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by in vivo growth curve data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Growth of parental P. berghei parasites was unaffected by the presence of ATc.
source: Conversely, growth of parental P. berghei parasites was unaffected by the presence of ATc (Figure 6a) as has been shown previously (Pino et al., 2012; Elsworth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by in vivo growth curve data shown in Figure 6a and citations to previous studies

claim: Parasites depleted of RhopH2 exhibited delayed progression to trophozoite stage.
source: Parasites in which RhopH2 had been depleted, exhibited delayed progression to trophozoite stage and the schizont stages displayed aberrant morphology, often appearing vacuolated and containing fewer merozoites (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: Supported by Giemsa-stained smear data shown in Figure 6b-c

claim: Schizont stages of parasites depleted of RhopH2 displayed aberrant morphology, often appearing vacuolated and containing fewer merozoites.
source: Parasites in which RhopH2 had been depleted, exhibited delayed progression to trophozoite stage and the schizont stages displayed aberrant morphology, often appearing vacuolated and containing fewer merozoites (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: Supported by Giemsa-stained smear data shown in Figure 6b-c

claim: Parasites depleted of RhopH2 could invade erythrocytes but exhibited a delay in the transition from the early to more mature trophozoite forms.
source: A synchronous in vitro invasion and growth assay using merozoites that had been generated from cultured schizonts confirmed these findings, showing that parasites depleted of RhopH2 could invade erythrocytes but exhibited a delay in the transition from the early to more mature trophozoite forms (Figure 6d), consistent with our findings in P. falciparum.
evidence: Supported by in vitro invasion and growth assay data shown in Figure 6d

claim: No defect in the export of PfEMP1, or trafficking of either RESA to the erythrocyte membrane or SBP1 to the Maurer's clefts was evident after knocking down RhopH2 expression.
source: However, no defect in the export of PfEMP1, or trafficking of either RESA to the erythrocyte membrane or SBP1 to the Maurer's clefts was evident after knocking down RhopH2 expression with GlcN (Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7a

claim: The localization of RhopH3 and to a lesser extent RhopH1/clag3 was affected when RhopH2 expression was knocked down.
source: In contrast, the localization of RhopH3 and to a lesser extent RhopH1/clag3 was affected when RhopH2 expression was knocked down (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: RhopH2-HAglmS parasites supplemented with 0.5 mM GlcN could similarly export a nanoluciferase reporter (Hyp1-NLuc) as RhopH2-HAglmS (-GlcN) or 3D7 parasites (±) GlcN.
source: Moreover, RhopH2-HAglmS parasites supplemented with a reduced concentration of 0.5 mM GlcN that still gave efficient RhopH2 knockdown (Figure 7b) and which were harvested at mid-trophozite stage before parasites growth was impaired (Figure 7c), could similarly export a nanoluciferase reporter (Hyp1-NLuc) as RhopH2-HAglmS (-GlcN) or 3D7 parasites (±) GlcN (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by nanoluciferase export assay data shown in Figure 7d

claim: GlcN-mediated knockdown of RhopH2 dramatically reduced the capacity of infected erythrocytes to be lysed by sorbitol.
source: We established that GlcN-mediated knockdown of RhopH2 dramatically reduced the capacity of infected erythrocytes to be lysed by sorbitol, suggesting RhopH2 contributes to NPP activity (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by sorbitol lysis assay data shown in Figure 8a

claim: 3D7-parasitized erythrocytes treated with GlcN were not affected in their ability to be lysed by sorbitol.
source: In contrast, 3D7-parasitized erythrocytes treated with GlcN were not affected in their ability to be lysed by sorbitol indicating that depletion of RhopH2 and not treatment with GlcN was responsible for inhibition of NPP function (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by sorbitol lysis assay data shown in Figure 8a

claim: When an iso-osmotic solution of alanine was used instead of sorbitol, increasing concentrations of GlcN reduced the capacity of RhopH2-HAglmS parasitized erythrocytes to be lysed.
source: When an iso-osmotic solution of alanine was used instead of sorbitol, similar results were obtained, with increasing concentrations of GlcN reducing the capacity of RhopH2-HAglmS parasitized erythrocytes to be lysed (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by alanine lysis assay data shown in Figure 8c

claim: More lysis inhibition was observed in 32 hr trophozoites compared to 24 hr trophozoites.
source: More lysis inhibition was also observed in 32 hr trophozoites compared to 24 hr trophozoites, consistent with the NPPs being more developed in older parasites.
evidence: Supported by alanine/sorbitol lysis assay data and established knowledge about NPP development

claim: Knockdown of RhopH2 causes a reproducible metabolic shift in the parasites.
source: A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of all metabolite features across the four sample groups, 3D7 ±GlcN) and RhopH2-HAglmS (±GlcN) showed that replicates from groups 3D7 (±GlcN) and RhopH2-HAglmS (-GlcN) clustered together, and that these were metabolically different to the induced RhopH2 knockdown, RhopH2-HAglmS (+GlcN) (Figure 9a). This indicates that knockdown of RhopH2 causes a reproducible metabolic shift in the parasites.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 9a

claim: The RhopH2 knockdown resulted in decreased levels of folate and thiamin phosphates.
source: A detailed scrutiny of individual metabolites showed that while glucosamine treatment appeared to elevate metabolite levels in general, the RhopH2 knockdown resulted in decreased levels of folate and thiamin phosphates, which are essential vitamins and cofactors for cellular growth (Figure 9c).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 9c

claim: Folate and thiamin phosphates are essential vitamins and cofactors for cellular growth.
source: A detailed scrutiny of individual metabolites showed that while glucosamine treatment appeared to elevate metabolite levels in general, the RhopH2 knockdown resulted in decreased levels of folate and thiamin phosphates, which are essential vitamins and cofactors for cellular growth (Figure 9c).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Intermediates in the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway (N-carbamoyl L-aspartate, dihydroorotate and orotate) significantly decreased upon RhopH2 depletion.
source: The other class of metabolites to significantly decrease upon RhopH2 depletion were intermediates in the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway, N-carbamoyl L-aspartate, dihydroorotate and orotate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data

claim: N-carbamoyl L-aspartate, dihydroorotate and orotate are essential nucleotide precursors in P. falciparum.
source: These metabolites are essential nucleotide precursors in P. falciparum, however, levels of downstream nucleotides were not affected at this time-point (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with reference to supplementary data

claim: Levels of downstream nucleotides were not affected at the time-point analyzed in the RhopH2 knockdown.
source: These metabolites are essential nucleotide precursors in P. falciparum, however, levels of downstream nucleotides were not affected at this time-point (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Supplementary file 1

claim: The glycolytic intermediates 3-phosphoglycerate and phosphoenolpyruvate were significantly and specifically depleted in the RhopH2 knockdown.
source: Few other metabolites were significantly and specifically depleted in the RhopH2 knockdown, with the exception of the glycolytic intermediates 3-phosphoglycerate and phosphoenolpyruvate (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Supplementary file 1

claim: The urea cycle intermediate argininosuccinate extensively accumulated (>5-fold higher than all controls) in the RhopH2 knockdown.
source: The only putatively identified metabolite to extensively accumulate (>5-fold higher than all controls) in the RhopH2 knockdown was the urea cycle intermediate argininosuccinate, however, the other urea cycle intermediates were not significantly perturbed.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data

claim: A general increase in amino acid levels was observed in the RhopH2 knockdown.
source: Interestingly, a general increase in amino acid levels was also observed in the RhopH2 knockdown (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 9d

claim: Levels of folate and phosphoenolpyruvate were significantly lower in furosemide-treated parasites.
source: Consistent with the RhopH2 knockdown, levels of folate and phosphoenolpyruvate were significantly lower in furosemide-treated parasites, and threonine, histidine, asparagine, serine and argininosuccinate levels all increased (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 9d

claim: Threonine, histidine, asparagine, serine and argininosuccinate levels all increased in furosemide-treated parasites.
source: Consistent with the RhopH2 knockdown, levels of folate and phosphoenolpyruvate were significantly lower in furosemide-treated parasites, and threonine, histidine, asparagine, serine and argininosuccinate levels all increased (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 9d

claim: The general depletion of de novo pyrimidine synthesis intermediates was not observed with furosemide.
source: Interestingly, the general depletion of de novo pyrimidine synthesis intermediates was not observed with furosemide, with N-carbamoyl L-aspartate levels found to be significantly higher following furosemide treatment.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data

claim: The RhopH2 synthesized during the schizont stage is carried into erythrocytes during invasion, initially localizing to the PVM.
source: In this study we have characterized RhopH2 expression and localization and investigated the consequences of knocking down RhopH2 expression on the parasite with the aim to infer function. We show that the RhopH2 synthesized during the schizont stage is carried into erythrocytes during invasion, initially localizing to the PVM.
evidence: Supported by the combined expression and localization data presented in the study

claim: From the PVM, RhopH2 then traffics through the erythrocyte cytoplasm until it reaches its final destination at the erythrocyte membrane.
source: From the PVM, RhopH2 then traffics through the erythrocyte cytoplasm until it reaches its final destination at the erythrocyte membrane.
evidence: Supported by the localization data presented in the study

claim: RhopH2 is not a Maurer's clefts resident protein per se.
source: Although RhopH2 localizes to punctate structures in the cytoplasm, the lack of co-localization with SBP1 indicates RhopH2 is not a Maurer's clefts resident protein per se.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of co-localization with SBP1

claim: The RhopH complex does not operate as a trafficking complex in a manner independent of PTEX to escort exported proteins throughout the erythrocyte cytoplasm.
source: Our results also indicate that the RhopH complex does not operate as a trafficking complex in a manner independent of PTEX to escort exported proteins throughout the erythrocyte cytoplasm (Ling et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the protein export data showing no defect upon RhopH2 knockdown

claim: Upon arriving at the erythrocyte membrane, RhopH2 associates with the host cytoskeleton through direct or indirect interactions with spectrin and/or ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.1 or protein 4.2.
source: Upon arriving at the erythrocyte membrane, RhopH2 associates with the host cytoskeleton through direct or indirect interactions with spectrin and/or ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.1 or protein 4.2, which are involved in tethering spectrin to the erythrocyte membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the immunoprecipitation data showing interactions with cytoskeletal proteins

claim: Depletion of RhopH2 in cycle one did not affect transition into cycle two, suggesting RhopH2 plays no direct role in invasion.
source: Depletion of RhopH2 in cycle one did not affect transition into cycle two, suggesting RhopH2 plays no direct role in invasion.
evidence: Inferred from the invasion assay data showing no effect on invasion efficiency

claim: NPP activity was greatly reduced upon RhopH2 knockdown.
source: However, NPP activity was greatly reduced and parasite growth slowed as parasites progressed into trophozoite stage in cycle two, possibly due to nutrient depravation and/or accumulation of waste products.
evidence: Supported by sorbitol and alanine lysis assay data

claim: Parasite growth slowed as parasites progressed into trophozoite stage in cycle two after RhopH2 knockdown, possibly due to nutrient deprivation and/or accumulation of waste products.
source: However, NPP activity was greatly reduced and parasite growth slowed as parasites progressed into trophozoite stage in cycle two, possibly due to nutrient depravation and/or accumulation of waste products.
evidence: Supported by growth data and speculative interpretation based on NPP function

claim: Transition into cycle three was curtailed by reduced schizont rupture and merozoite malformation that may be linked to reduced de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
source: Transition into cycle three was curtailed by interesting phenomena including reduced schizont rupture and merozoite malformation that may be linked to reduced de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
evidence: Supported by growth data, video microscopy, and metabolomics data with speculative interpretation

claim: RhopH2 appears to be important for NPP activity and for the exchange of nutrients and wastes with the blood plasma to facilitate parasite growth and proliferation.
source: Taken together, RhopH2 appears to be important for NPP activity and for the exchange of nutrients and wastes with the blood plasma to facilitate parasite growth and proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on NPP activity, metabolomics, and growth phenotypes

claim: The reduction in the levels of folate in the RhopH2 knockdown implicates RhopH2 in nutrient uptake.
source: The reduction in the levels of folate in the RhopH2 knockdown was also striking and implicates RhopH2 in nutrient uptake.
evidence: Inferred from the metabolomics data showing decreased folate levels

claim: P. falciparum is capable of folate synthesis but also needs to import exogenous folate.
source: Although P. falciparum is capable of folate synthesis, it also needs to import exogenous folate (Krungkrai et al., 1989; Wang et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: P. falciparum encodes for two folate transporters FT1 and FT2, which localize to the plasma membrane.
source: and encodes for two folate transporters FT1 (PF3D7_0828600) and FT2 (PF3D7_1116500), which localize to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: RhopH2 and FT1 have very similar expression profiles, with maximal expression observed in the late trophozoite and schizont stage.
source: RhopH2 and FT1 have very similar expression profiles (Aurrecoechea et al., 2009), with maximal expression observed in the late trophozoite and schizont stage.
evidence: Supported by citation to Aurrecoechea et al., 2009

claim: It is conceivable that RhopH2 and FT1 act in concert to facilitate the transport of folate across the erythrocyte membrane and parasite plasma membrane, respectively.
source: It is conceivable that RhopH2 and FT1 act in concert to facilitate the transport of folate across the erythrocyte membrane, and parasite plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on expression profiles and folate depletion data

claim: A similar decrease in folate levels observed in furosemide-treated parasites provides support for implication of RhopH2 in NPP mediated nutrient uptake.
source: A similar decrease in folate levels observed in furosemide-treated parasites provides support for implication of RhopH2 in NPP mediated nutrient uptake.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data comparing RhopH2 knockdown and furosemide treatment

claim: The combined reductions in folate uptake and de novo pyrimidine synthesis in RhopH2 depleted parasites is likely to lead to decreased availability of pyrimidine nucleotides once pre-existing pools are depleted.
source: The combined reductions in folate uptake (an essential cofactor for thymine nucleotide synthesis) and de novo pyrimidine synthesis in RhopH2 depleted parasites is likely to lead to decreased availability of pyrimidine nucleotides once pre-existing pools are depleted, which may explain the reduced number of merozoites and delayed growth phenotype observed in the RhopH2 knockdown.
evidence: Inferred from the metabolomics data and growth phenotypes with speculative interpretation

claim: The reduced number of merozoites and delayed growth phenotype observed in the RhopH2 knockdown may be explained by decreased availability of pyrimidine nucleotides.
source: The combined reductions in folate uptake (an essential cofactor for thymine nucleotide synthesis) and de novo pyrimidine synthesis in RhopH2 depleted parasites is likely to lead to decreased availability of pyrimidine nucleotides once pre-existing pools are depleted, which may explain the reduced number of merozoites and delayed growth phenotype observed in the RhopH2 knockdown.
evidence: Speculative interpretation linking metabolomics data to growth phenotypes

claim: This phenotype has been reported earlier in metabolically compromised P. berghei parasites with a disrupted pyrimidine synthesis pathway.
source: This phenotype has been reported earlier in metabolically compromised P. berghei parasites with a disrupted pyrimidine synthesis pathway (Srivastava et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srivastava et al., 2015

claim: The observed increase in amino acids in the RhopH2 knockdown could be due to a reduced efflux of excess amino acids produced by haemoglobin digestion.
source: The observed increase in amino acids in the RhopH2 knockdown could be due to a reduced efflux of excess amino acids produced by haemoglobin digestion (Krugliak et al., 2002), which may otherwise render the infected cells susceptible to osmotic challenge or, alternatively, increased protein degradation to survive nutrient starvation, in a manner analogous to that observed following isoleucine starvation (Babbitt et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of metabolomics data with citations to previous studies

claim: Depletion of RhopH2 in P. berghei had a drastic consequence on parasite growth in mice.
source: It should also be noted that depletion of RhopH2 in P. berghei had a drastic consequence on parasite growth in mice, but when the parasites were cultured ex vivo the growth delays and aberrant parasite morphology were always less striking.
evidence: Supported by in vivo and ex vivo growth data

claim: The nutrients supplied to the parasites in culture are likely to be in greater abundance than what is available to the parasites in vivo.
source: This may be because the nutrients supplied to the parasites in culture are likely to be in greater abundance than what is available to the parasites in vivo (Pillai et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation to Pillai et al., 2012

claim: That RhopH2 can be extracted from membranes using carbonate provides little support for RhopH2 being an integral membrane protein and a channel in the erythrocyte membrane through which solutes are transported.
source: That RhopH2 can be extracted from membranes using carbonate provides little support for RhopH2 being an integral membrane protein and a channel in the erythrocyte membrane through which solutes are transported.
evidence: Inferred from the solubility assay data

claim: This work provides the first direct genetic evidence that depletion of a member of the RhopH complex leads to altered NPP function.
source: In summary, our work reveals that the RhopH complex interacts with components of the erythrocyte cytoskeleton as well as numerous exported proteins that are involved in host cell remodeling and a schematic illustrating how the RhopH complex may traffic to the erythrocyte surface is provided in Figure 10. We provide the first direct genetic evidence that depletion of a member of the RhopH complex leads to altered NPP function, and depletion of essential vitamins and cofactors.
evidence: Supported by the combined genetic knockdown and NPP activity data

claim: Depletion of RhopH2 leads to depletion of essential vitamins and cofactors.
source: We provide the first direct genetic evidence that depletion of a member of the RhopH complex leads to altered NPP function, and depletion of essential vitamins and cofactors.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data

claim: The alteration to parasite growth and metabolism, as well as the effect on parasite replication and delayed egress, are in keeping with the NPPs being an important erythrocyte modification induced by the parasite.
source: The alteration to parasite growth and metabolism, as well as the effect on parasite replication and delayed egress, are in keeping with the NPPs being an important erythrocyte modification induced by the parasite.
evidence: Inferred from the combined phenotypic and metabolomics data
